reduction.statement: for N >= 2, x^x = N has exactly one positive real root x, and for whole numbers 1 <= q <= p: p/q < x iff p^p < N^q·q^p, p/q <= x iff p^p <= N^q·q^p, x < p/q iff N^q·q^p < p^p, x <= p/q iff N^q·q^p <= p^p; at q = 1, k <= x iff k^k <= N and x <= k iff N <= k^k
reduction.rests on: x^x <= 1 on (0, 1], x^x strictly increasing on [1, oo)
reduction.read: the negative-base convention: every theorem is about positive reals (Mathlib's Real.rpow); that a negative x is not a root worth counting is a reading of the problem (claimbox/library/selfpower.py), not decided here

theorems.note: a fraction p/q > 1 in lowest terms has 1 <= q < p, a whole bound k >= 1 is q = 1: both inside the theorems' 1 <= q <= p

own.standing: cert-machine's own claims, through the same decider; claimbox stated none of them

rows.statement: the root of xˣ = 64 is transcendental
rows.origin: cert-machine's own claim (added 2026-10-31): not claimbox's, not the AI model's
rows.reason: This decider answers one question: does the root lie above or below a given fraction, by one comparison of two whole numbers. "Transcendental" says the root is a root of no polynomial with integer coefficients: infinitely many polynomials, not one comparison, and no number of decided brackets reaches it.
rows.trueBy: Cited, not decided: the root is not a fraction (p/q in lowest terms with q > 1 would give p^p = 64^q·q^p, which q cannot divide, and no whole k has k^k = 64), and an irrational algebraic x would make x^x transcendental by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem, while 64 is not.
rows.decidableBy: A kernel-checked proof: the Gelfond–Schneider theorem formalized (Mathlib at the pin of lean/xx-reduction, d13f23b7, holds no Gelfond–Schneider theorem), then the two-line argument above in Lean on top of XXReduction.existsUnique_root. With that, it is a theorem to check, not a comparison to compute.
rows.why: not a comparison of the root with one fraction, the one statement this decider reads
